content.title: Defining Variables from Real-World Contexts
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the foundational step of algebraic modeling: identifying a single unknown quantity from a word problem and assigning it a symbol with a clear unit and domain.
learning_objectives: Identify the single concrete quantity to be counted or measured in a word problem.
Assign a symbol to a variable and define it using specific units.
Determine the domain constraints of a variable, such as nonnegativity or integer requirements.

sections.title: The Name-and-Unit Strategy
sections.content:
When starting an ACT algebra problem, you must define your variable precisely. A variable should represent a single, concrete quantity that can be measured (like weight or time) or counted (like people or items). A complete definition includes three parts: the symbol (usually x, n, or t), the specific quantity being tracked, and the unit of measurement. For example, instead of saying 'x is coffee,' say 'x = the number of pounds of coffee beans.'

![A flowchart showing the steps to define a variable: Identify Quantity, Assign Symbol and Unit, and Check Constraints.](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/b2bacf88-c257-4e51-b83d-4da2ada2bf62-1786505773670-792.webp)

sections.title: Identifying the Unknown
sections.content: Look for the specific value the problem asks for or the value that other quantities depend on. If a problem mentions two different items, choose one as your primary variable. The goal is to turn a vague situation into a countable or measurable number. Avoid defining variables as 'total cost' or 'total weight' if those values are actually the result of a calculation involving a simpler count.

sections.title: Domain and Constraints
sections.content: Every real-world variable has a domain—the set of possible values it can take. Common constraints include: 1. Nonnegativity: Most physical quantities (distance, count, time) cannot be negative. 2. Integers: If you are counting discrete items like people, cars, or bags, the variable must be a whole number. 3. Logical Bounds: If there are 50 total items, the variable representing one type of item cannot exceed 50.

worked_examples.question: A theater sells adult tickets for $15 and child tickets for $10. On Saturday, the theater sold 300 tickets total. Which choice best defines a variable to help determine the revenue from child tickets?
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Identify the unknown. We need to know how many of each ticket type were sold. Step 2: Assign symbol and meaning. Let c = the number of child tickets sold. The unit is 'tickets.' Step 3: Check constraints. The value of c must be an integer (you can't sell half a ticket) and must be between 0 and 300. Therefore, 'c = the number of child tickets sold' is the best definition.

common_mistakes: Defining a variable as a category (e.g., 'x = apples') instead of a quantity (e.g., 'x = the number of apples').
Mixing units, such as defining a variable in minutes when the rest of the problem uses hours.
Choosing a derived quantity (like total cost) as the variable instead of the base quantity (like number of items) that determines the cost.
exam_tips: Read the final question of the word problem first; it often tells you exactly what the variable should represent.
Perform a 'Substitution Test': Replace the variable in your equation with your written definition. If the sentence sounds like nonsense, your definition is too vague.
Watch for 'integer constraints' in problems involving people or distinct objects.
content.recap: To define a variable, identify one specific countable or measurable quantity, assign it a symbol, state its units clearly, and ensure its possible values (domain) match the real-world context.

knowledge_claims.content: To define a variable, first identify a single concrete quantity to count or measure from the context.
A complete variable definition must include a symbol, the quantity it represents, and the unit of measurement.
The 'Substitution Test' involves replacing the symbol in an equation with its full word definition to ensure the logic holds.
Variables representing counts of discrete objects, such as people or bags, must be restricted to integer values.
Physical quantities like distance, time, and counts in real-world modeling are typically constrained to be nonnegative.
It is a mistake to define a variable as a general category (e.g., 'x = large bags') rather than a specific quantity (e.g., 'x = the number of large bags').
A base quantity (like number of items) is usually a better variable choice than a derived quantity (like total weight) because it simplifies constraints.
The final sentence of an ACT word problem often provides the best cue for what the variable should represent.
A variable's domain is the set of all possible values it can logically take within the constraints of the problem.
If a problem involves a total limit (e.g., 240 total bags), the variable representing a subset must be bounded by that total.
When multiple unknowns exist, choose one as the primary variable and express others in terms of that variable.
Always verify that the units of the defined variable are consistent with the units used in the rest of the problem's constants.

items.stem:
Practice form 1.
A taxi charges $2 plus $3 per mile. Which variable definition is most useful?
A) Let m be the number of miles traveled.
B) Let m be the color of the taxi.
C) Let m be the driver's name.
D) Let m be an unrelated date.

options.A: Let m be the number of miles traveled.
options.B: Let m be the color of the taxi.
options.C: Let m be the driver's name.
options.D: Let m be an unrelated date.

items.explanation: The variable should represent the changing quantity in the model.

videoLesson.title: Define a Name-and-Unit Variable
videoLesson.description: You will recognize the single concrete quantity to count or measure and its unit. Assign a short symbol with its unit in words and check domain constraints (nonnegative, integer).
